description: Seven privacy-by-design principles with engineer-facing scoring criteria

principles.name: Proactive not reactive; preventative not remedial

criteria.question: Was a privacy or threat review done before build started?
Has high-risk processing been identified, and is a DPIA planned if needed?
Are known privacy issues scheduled to be fixed before go-live, not after an incident?
Are optional features that collect extra personal data off by default?
Is extra collection opt-in rather than opt-out?
Do new accounts and roles start at least privilege?
Are privacy controls in the architecture, not only in a policy document?
Are privacy requirements written into the design, not added after launch?
Can the product goal be met without dropping privacy or security controls?
Is there a working fallback that does not require the higher-risk data (for example typed notes instead of a full recording)?
Is personal data encrypted in transit and at rest?
Is admin access role-based, with MFA for privileged roles?
Is there a defined, enforced way to delete or dispose of personal data at end of life?
Is access to sensitive personal data logged?

principles.name: Visibility and transparency — keep it open

criteria.question: Is there a clear privacy notice for the people this system is about?
Is this processing recorded (for example on a ROPA)?
Can the organisation show who decided the design and what was accepted?

principles.name: Respect for user privacy — keep it user-centric

criteria.question: Is there a way to handle access, erasure, and similar rights for this data?
If the system makes a significant decision about someone, can a human review it?
Can the person use the system without the higher-risk option (for example join without recording)?
